title: Gospel Authorship and Dating
subtitle: What mainstream biblical scholarship says about who wrote the Gospels and when — compared with the Quran's single-generation compilation
summary: The canonical Gospels are ancient sources for Jesus, but the texts themselves do not name their authors in their opening narratives, and their traditional titles were attached through early church transmission. Most modern scholars date them decades after Jesus. This does not make them worthless; it does mean that their distance, dependence, and theological aims should be weighed when they conflict with the Quran's claim to be preserved revelation.

seo.metaTitle: Gospel Authorship and Dating: What Scholars Really Say
seo.metaDescription: The four Gospels are the main narrative sources for Jesus, but the texts themselves do not name their authors in their opening lines.

sections.title: The Evidence in Brief
sections.body: The four Gospels are the main narratives about Jesus. Their opening lines do not name their authors. Traditional names appear in early church testimony. Many modern scholars date the final texts between about 70 and 100 CE. They debate how directly the texts preserve eyewitness testimony. The Quran presents a different model. It was publicly recited and memorized during Muhammad’s lifetime.

sections.title: What the Gospels Claim About Their Sources
sections.body: The Gospels do not begin with the modern formula “written by Matthew, Mark, Luke, or John.” Luke describes collecting earlier reports (Luke 1:1–4). Early church testimony connects the books with the traditional names. Many Christians defend those attributions. Modern scholars study that testimony and the internal evidence.

sections.title: One Voice, One Generation
sections.body:
Islam frames textual origin differently. Muslims believe the Quran came through one prophet over about twenty-three years. Quran 4:82 invites readers to examine its consistency: “If it had been from [any] other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction.”

The Quran was memorized as it was revealed. It was gathered into one written form within a generation. Muslims therefore see one public voice, not a later patchwork of unnamed authors. The historical claim is clear and testable.

sections.title: What Mainstream Scholarship Concludes
sections.body:
Luke says he traced earlier reports and eyewitness testimony (Luke 1:1–4). He presents himself as an investigator, not a named eyewitness. John closes with a testimony about the disciple and uses “we” (John 21:24–25). Many scholars see a community or later editor in that ending.

Common scholarly dates place Mark around 65–75 CE, Matthew and Luke around 80–90 CE, and John around 90–100 CE. These dates are debated. They still place the final texts decades after Jesus. Questions about authorship, sources, and theological development therefore remain open.

sections.title: Why Authorship and Date Matter
sections.body: A later or unnamed author can preserve real history. Anonymity does not prove falsehood. It does affect how directly a saying can be traced to Jesus. The Quran offers another model. A named messenger recited it publicly. His community memorized it. Written copies were standardized early.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
Anonymous authorship does not mean the Gospels contain no history. Many scholars see earlier traditions behind them. Historical value and authorship are related, but they are not the same question.

The dating and anonymity discussion is mainstream scholarship. It is not an attack invented by Muslims.

The Islamic hadith system also does not make every report authentic. Muslim scholars used chains, narrator criticism, and grades. Traditional Gospel names can remain useful labels while the documents themselves do not prove their authors.

sections.title: The Quran as the Final Criterion
sections.body: Islam honors the Gospel originally given to Jesus. It distinguishes that revelation from later biographies about him. The Gospels preserve valuable memories and teachings. Their authorship and development still require judgment. The Quran is a direct, named revelation. It confirms Jesus, corrects claims about him, and calls humanity to worship God alone.

sections.title: The Central Takeaway
sections.body: The Gospels deserve serious reading. Their authorship and dating also call for care when later theology is placed above Jesus’ clear worship of one God. Islam honors Jesus as Messiah and messenger. It preserves the simpler call to worship the Lord he worshiped.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Are the traditional Gospel authors certain?
A: The names are early and important. The texts themselves do not state them in their opening lines. Scholars debate how the traditional attributions arose.

Q: Do later dates make the Gospels worthless?
A: No. A later source can preserve earlier material. Dating helps readers judge how claims were transmitted.

Q: Does Islam reject everything in the Gospels?
A: No. Islam affirms the original Gospel and accepts truths that remain consistent with revelation. The Quran is the final criterion.

Q: Why does authorship matter?
A: It affects how directly a saying can be linked to Jesus.

Q: What is the Islamic alternative?
A: The Quran was recited by one named messenger, memorized publicly, and written during his lifetime. The traditional revelation period lasted about twenty-three years; Uthman's standardization followed roughly two decades after Muhammad's death.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
Selected sources and further reading:

- **Jesus, Interrupted. Revealing the Hidden Contradictions in the Bible (And Why We Don't Know About Them)**. Bart D. Ehrman. A widely read overview of mainstream scholarly conclusions on Gospel authorship, dating. And the Synoptic Problem.
- **An Introduction to the New Testament**. Raymond E. Brown. A standard Catholic scholarly textbook surveying authorship and dating debates for each New Testament book.
- **The Historical Figure of Jesus**. E. P. Sanders. A leading historical-Jesus scholar's discussion of the Gospel sources and their reliability.
- **Hadith. Muhammad's Legacy in the Medieval and Modern World**. Jonathan A. C. Brown. An accessible academic overview of isnad methodology and the development of hadith criticism.
- **Hadith Literature. Its Origin, Development and Special Features**. M. Zubayr Siddiqi. A classic account of the science of hadith transmission and chain evaluation.

bibleVerses.text: Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative concerning those matters which have been fulfilled among us, even as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus; that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed.

This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things. We know that his witness is true. There are also many other things which Jesus did, which if they would all be written, I suppose that even the world itself wouldn’t have room for the books that would be written.

faq.question: Does saying the Gospels are "anonymous" mean nobody knows anything about who wrote them?
faq.answer: The narratives do not directly name their authors, while manuscript titles and early church testimony attribute them to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Many scholars argue that the names were attached later. Others, including [Simon Gathercole](https://academic.oup.com/jts/article-abstract/69/2/447/5101372), argue that early attributions could have accompanied the texts. Internal anonymity, titles, and actual authorship are related questions, but they are not identical.

faq.question: Isn't the idea that the Gospels were written decades later just an anti-Christian argument?
faq.answer: No. This dating and the anonymous-authorship conclusion are standard positions in mainstream New Testament scholarship, taught in Christian seminaries and secular universities alike, and defended by many devout Christian scholars as part of honest textual criticism.

faq.question: How is the isnad system different from just trusting oral tradition generally?
faq.answer: Isnad requires every report to carry a named, checkable chain of transmitters, each evaluated for reliability, memory, and plausible contact with the next link, and reports are formally graded rather than simply accepted.

faq.question: Does the Quran's single-generation compilation mean it has no textual history at all?
faq.answer: It has a documented history of public memorization and writing during Muhammad's lifetime, followed by collection and standardization. The traditional revelation period lasted about twenty-three years. Uthman's standardization occurred roughly two decades after the Prophet's death, so the broader sequence spans about four decades.

faq.question: Why does this comparison matter for someone deciding what to believe?
faq.answer: It does not settle every theological question on its own, but it gives a concrete, checkable basis for comparing how each tradition documents the distance between its claimed source and the text available today.
